title: Bible Study Ring
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
stem:
Question ID: 14731_bible_study_ring

Peter gave Mary a diamond engagement ring after their law-school Bible study group celebrated their engagement. Mary later broke off the engagement but refused to return the ring. One night after midnight, Peter entered Mary’s townhouse to retrieve the ring. Mary was not at home, but John, a neighbor, saw Peter enter and called the police. Peter searched for the ring for 10 minutes but did not find it. As Peter was walking out the front door, the police arrived and immediately arrested him.

Peter has been charged with burglary in a jurisdiction that follows the common law. Which of the following, if proved, would serve as Peter’s best defense to the charge?
call: Peter has been charged with burglary in a jurisdiction that follows the common law. Which of the following, if proved, would serve as Peter’s best defense to the charge?

choices.A: Peter knew that Mary kept a spare key under a clay jar by the front door and used the key to enter the townhouse.
choices.B: Peter incorrectly and unreasonably believed that he was legally entitled to the ring.
choices.C: Peter knew that Mary was away overnight when he entered the townhouse.
choices.D: Peter left the townhouse without taking anything of value.

rightExplanation:
B is correct. The question asks for the best defense to common-law burglary. The live element is not whether Peter found the ring. It is whether, when he entered, he had the intent to commit the underlying felony, here larceny.

Gold Key: If common-law burglary is charged through intended larceny, an honest claim of right to the specific property negates larcenous intent, even if the belief is mistaken or unreasonable.

Silver Key: In a burglary-defense answer array, separate the choices by what element they attack. The answer that attacks intent at entry beats choices about entry method, occupancy, or completion.

wrongExplanations.A: Using a spare key is not the best defense. It attacks the entry/breaking side of burglary, but the fact does not show consent or legal authority to enter. Gold Key: the key-under-the-mat fact does not defeat burglary unless it shows permission; merely knowing where a key is kept does not make the entry authorized.
wrongExplanations.C: Knowing Mary was away does not defeat common-law burglary. The trap is thinking burglary requires a person to be inside the dwelling. Gold Key: common-law burglary focuses on the dwelling, nighttime entry, and intent at entry; actual occupancy at that moment is not the defense.
wrongExplanations.D: Leaving empty-handed does not defeat burglary. Burglary is complete when the defendant breaks and enters with the required intent. The intended felony need not be completed. Silver Key: do not pick a post-entry-result fact when the charge turns on intent at entry.

c3.label: CUT
c3.text:
* A attacks access method. It does not answer the intent problem. Keep only until the burglary-entry Gold Key kills it.
* C attacks occupancy. It does not answer the charged element that matters.
* D attacks success/completion. It does not answer intent at entry.

c3.label: CLASH
c3.text:
The array is not a clean two-answer clash. It is a four-fact best-defense array:

* A = entry method.
* B = intent/claim of right.
* C = occupancy.
* D = completed theft.

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: Apply the Gold Key: common-law burglary charged through larceny turns on intent to commit larceny at entry. B is the only fact that defeats that intent.

studentScript: Best defense to burglary. Sort by element. A is entry method. C is occupancy. D is completion. B is intent. Gold Key: claim of right kills larceny intent. Pick B.

A.signal: The fact attacks how Peter got in, not whether he had larcenous intent at entry.
A.lawyer: Using a hidden spare key without permission does not itself supply authority to enter or defeat common-law burglary.

B.signal: This is the only fact that targets the required intent behind the intended larceny.
B.lawyer: An honest claim of right to the specific property negates larcenous intent even if mistaken or unreasonable.

C.signal: The fact attacks whether someone was home, not the burglary intent element.
C.lawyer: Common-law burglary does not require the dwelling to be occupied at the moment of entry.

D.signal: The fact attacks whether the intended theft succeeded, not whether Peter entered with the required intent.
D.lawyer: Burglary is complete upon the required entry with the required intent; the underlying felony need not be completed.

goldKeys.trigger: Defendant enters to retrieve a specific item he believes is his.
goldKeys.unlocks: Why B is the best defense.
goldKeys.authority: LII Wex larceny; Commonwealth v. Liebenow; People v. Green

goldKeys.statement: Common-law burglary is complete at the unauthorized nighttime entry of a dwelling with intent to commit a felony inside; the intended felony need not be completed.
goldKeys.trigger: Answer focuses on leaving empty-handed or not taking property.
goldKeys.unlocks: Why D is not a defense.
goldKeys.authority: LII Wex breaking and entering / burglary

goldKeys.unlocks: Why A is the dominant wrong-answer trap.

remediation.title: Burglary defense = attack the entry-time intent
remediation.signal: Question asks best defense to common-law burglary.
remediation.studentMove: Sort the answer choices by the element each one attacks.
remediation.tinyRule: If the burglary theory is intended larceny, a claim-of-right fact attacks intent.
remediation.trap: Picking key use, empty house, or no completed theft.
